title: Lesson 92 - What We Know—and What We Don't

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: What we know is that all three hundred selected public records were copied into the separate test area and the source catalog remained unchanged.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: The log also shows eighteen structural warnings: twelve unusual but valid date formats, four missing creator fields and two duplicate item numbers.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: Can we say eighteen records were wrong?

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: No. We can rule out that interpretation because twelve warnings were confirmed as valid exceptions. Four records lacked creator data in the source, and the two duplicate numbers require further review.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: The evidence suggests the automated checks found useful review targets, but it does not give us an eighteen-record error rate.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: Correct. In the sixty-record manual sample, fifty-seven test records matched the source exactly and three had title-punctuation differences caused by one mapping rule.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: That rule has now been corrected, and the same sixty records passed a second comparison.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: Yes, but I’d be careful about saying the full catalog will therefore migrate accurately. This sample did not include restricted records or every description pattern.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: What we don’t know yet is how many additional mapping patterns appear in the remaining records.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: We also do not know whether the test response time will hold during peak public use.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: The median response time was 1.4 seconds across 120 prepared searches. Can we call the new search fast?

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: Only for those searches in that test environment. We can’t rule out slower performance with more users, larger indexes or different queries.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: Staff recorded eleven hours of parallel review. The examples don’t represent a full migration, so multiplying eleven hours by the number of batches would be unreliable.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: Exactly. Both experts agree that the safeguards worked as designed in this test. Where they differ is still the post-test migration sequence.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: The safest conclusion is that the process protected the source and identified a correctable mapping rule in this batch.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: Add that the test does not yet establish the best full-migration strategy, total staff time, restricted-record handling or peak performance.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: A more accurate way to put the recommendation is: run a second, more varied public-record batch before choosing between phased and single cutover.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: That may reduce some uncertainty, but it will not answer the restricted-record question. That requires a separate access review.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: I’ll mark the completed batch and corrected rule as closed; migration sequence, scaling and restricted access remain open.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: Good. The brief should let a reader see the evidence, the inference, the exceptions and the next decision without treating caution as failure.

transfer.title: Sofia's independent review message
transfer.instruction: Listen twice without reading. Record the two confirmed results, why eighteen warnings are not eighteen errors, the limited performance result and the two recommended next steps before giving a sourced 60-second summary.
transfer.speaker: Sofia
